summary: Registers "image" as a top-level media type for the Session Description Protocol. It is mainly used by SDP to negotiate and set up T.38 media streams, which carry fax over IP.

eli5.summary: When devices set up a call, they describe the kinds of data they will send. This adds "image" to the list, which is mostly used for sending fax over the internet.

subtitle: Registering 'image' as a top-level media type for session descriptions.

tldr.problem: The Session Description Protocol (SDP) defined in RFC 4566 omitted 'image' from its list of top-level media types, even though it was already widely used in practice for T.38 fax over IP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6466 formally registers 'image' as a top-level media type in the SDP Parameters registry maintained by IANA, bringing the registry in line with actual usage.
tldr.outcome: This registration ensures consistency between SDP and MIME media types and provides a standards-track justification for using 'image' in SDP session descriptions.

today: RFC 6466 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. The 'image' media type is now an official top-level media type in the SDP Parameters registry.

sections.title: Why 'image' Matters in SDP
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) is used to describe multimedia sessions, allowing devices to agree on what kinds of data they will exchange. RFC 4566 defined five top-level media types for SDP: 'audio', 'video', 'text', 'application', and 'message'. However, an important media type was missing: 'image'.

The 'image' media type is an established top-level MIME media type, and it was already widely used in real-world SDP implementations for negotiating T.38 fax media streams. ITU-T T.38 is a standard for sending fax documents over IP networks, and implementations commonly used 'image' in SDP descriptions even though the protocol specification did not officially register it.
sections.eli5: Imagine a rulebook for describing calls that was missing 'pictures' even though everyone was already sending pictures. This RFC fixes that.

sections.title: The Gap Between Standards and Practice
sections.content:
Before RFC 6466, a discrepancy existed between the SDP specification and real-world deployments. The specification created a registry for SDP-specific media types, separate from MIME types, and RFC 4566 was careful to request that new media types be registered in this registry. However, the 'image' type—which predated this registry decision—was not included in the initial list.

The RFC notes that 'image' had been extensively referenced in ITU-T T.38 examples and in IETF standards like RFC 4145 (TCP-Based Media Transport in SDP). The example in RFC 6466 shows a typical SDP session description for a T.38 fax media stream, with the media line reading m=image 49170 udptl t38. This usage was common, but lacked explicit standardization.
sections.eli5: The standard rulebook didn't mention 'pictures', but everyone was using them anyway. This RFC officially adds them to the book.

sections.title: IANA Registration Details
sections.content:
RFC 6466 registers 'image' as a media type in the Session Description Protocols (SDP) Parameters registry. The registration includes: the contact information of the registrant (Gonzalo Salgueiro from Cisco); the name to be registered in SDP as 'image'; the long-form name in English, also 'image'; the type of name as 'media' (not 'proto', 'fmt', or other variants); and the purpose of the registration.

The stated purpose is that the 'image' media type describes a media stream whose content consists of one or more separate images that require appropriate hardware to display. The media subtype (the part after the slash, such as 't38') further specifies the format. The registration notes that 'image' is used ubiquitously with the SIP control protocol to establish T.38 media streams.
sections.eli5: The registry now officially says: 'image' is a valid choice for describing media in a session, mainly for fax.

sections.title: Security and Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 6466 notes that registering 'image' as an SDP media type does not introduce new security considerations beyond those already described in RFC 4566. The security properties of SDP itself—and the Offer/Answer Model that negotiates these media types—remain unchanged.

However, the RFC acknowledges security issues in the technologies that might use this media type. T.38 itself, along with its transport protocols (TCP, UDP, and RTP), have documented security considerations. Additionally, the ability to exchange images other than T.38 could expose recipients to potentially malicious executable code. These risks are pre-existing and not introduced by this registration.
sections.eli5: Adding 'image' doesn't make calling less safe. But if someone sends you a bad image file, that's still dangerous. The RFC says so.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
This registration serves as formal standards-track justification for a media type that was already in widespread use. By registering 'image', RFC 6466 complies with the request in RFC 4566 Section 8.2.1, which stated that new top-level media types for SDP should be produced as Standards Track RFCs with good justification.

The practical benefit is alignment between the MIME media type namespace and the SDP media type registry. Implementors and specification writers can now point to a formal standards document when using 'image' in SDP. For T.38 fax over IP, this provides clearer guidance in the standards literature.
sections.eli5: This gives the rulebook permission to use 'image', which helps engineers know they're doing the right thing.
